implementation_notes: context.Context is the carrier and the convention: WithDeadline/WithTimeout derive a child whose deadline is the sooner of now+timeout and the parent's deadline, Done() closes when the budget expires, and Err() reports context.DeadlineExceeded or context.Canceled. The community rule that ctx is the first parameter of every function doing I/O makes propagation the default path rather than an add-on - net/http, database/sql and all gRPC clients honour it - so a hop computes the remaining time from ctx.Deadline() and derives its own WithTimeout from the incoming ctx instead of a fresh constant. gRPC-Go propagates deadlines between services automatically, and http.Request.Context() carries client disconnects into the handler tree.
pitfalls: Deriving context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), d) inside a handler drops the incoming deadline entirely; always derive from the request context.
Every WithCancel/WithTimeout cancels func must be called (defer cancel()): otherwise the timer and child context survive until the parent dies (go vet's lostcancel).
Storing a context in a struct or handing context.Background() to goroutines that outlive the handler defeats cancellation; pass the request ctx and stop workers on ctx.Done().
After an error, check ctx.Err() to distinguish DeadlineExceeded from Canceled, or a client cancellation is reported as a local timeout.
Never smuggle a deadline through context.WithValue: use the real deadline, which WithTimeout/WithDeadline propagate and every library already understands.
